newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS-Swedish PM says EMU could lead to federation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Swedish PM says EMU could lead to federation.

text.p: As Euro-scepticism grows in Sweden, Prime Minister Goran Persson has fuelled concern that Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) could transform the European Union into a federation with uniform fiscal policies.

In a column in the daily newspaper Svenska Dagbladet, Persson said that if fiscal policies became a union matter, the EU would become a federation, quite different from what was envisaged when Swedes voted to join.
"The EU would be transformed to something completely different than the EU the Swedish people, after some agony and a long and trying debate, approved (in a November 1994 referendum)," Persson said.
He refrained from saying whether he was for or against EMU but urged a discussion on what monetary union would really mean.
He called for a discussion on whether EMU would lift fiscal policies to EU levels or if a planned budget stability pact would suffice to counterbalance the power of a central bank.
"The third phase of the single currency union means that the balance between the economic and political players in Europe might change," Persson said.
"The common, strong and independent central bank that will handle the common monetary policy on its own might lack a counterbalancing force in European fiscal policies."
Since the referendum and Swedish membership of the EU from the start of 1995, Swedes have become more and more apprehensive about the union.

A poll last Saturday indicated that opposition to EMU was growing. According to the survey by pollster Temo, 44 percent of 1,000 people questioned in November and December were negative on EMU, up from 38 percent in October. Less than a third of Swedes were positive about joining EMU and the rest undecided.
Meanwhile, a Sunday poll suggested that public support for Persson's ruling Social Democrats fell by 3.1 percentage points to 29.6 percent in December, the lowest level since April 1991.
However, support for the opposition conservative party, the Moderates, rose by 2.7 percentage points to 29.1 percent.
This is the first time for years that support for the two largest parties has been almost level, according to the survey, conducted by the Swedish institute for Public Opinion and Research, Sifo.

Increased hostility towards EMU and the government has been linked as the Social Democrats have implemented tough budget cuts to meet Maastricht Treaty criteria for joining a single currency, making many Swedes blame EMU for their hardships.
The budget is now in such good shape that the country will meet the necessary criteria, Persson said in his column.

Although Persson and the government have argued that it is even more urgent for a country deciding to remain outside the EMU to meet the economic criteria, rather than being at the mercy of financial markets, many Swedes disagree.

The usually placid Swedes have demonstrated against the budget cuts, the easing of labour market laws to give employers more flexibility in hiring staff and unemployment at a previously unheard of level of 7.9 percent.

The Centre Party, the government's cooperation partner, is opposed to EMU on the grounds that it would lead to a federation. With strong public and political opposition, Persson keeps backing down on EMU.
When he was finance minister he said that he personally favoured EMU. But since becoming prime minister in mid-March this year, he has not expressed any preferences on the issue.
